title: Bamiyan
hookLine: the great Buddhas carved in an Afghan cliff, and destroyed

lines: A CLIFF IN AN AFGHAN VALLEY.
cards: In a green valley in the mountains of Afghanistan, a visitor stands at the foot of a tall cliff of soft, tan rock and looks up.
Cut into its face are two enormous hollows, arched at the top, each the shape of a standing figure. Inside them, nothing. Rubble at the bottom, sky on the stone.
For a long time those hollows held two great Buddhas, carved from the cliff itself, looking out over the valley. Now they hold their own absence.

teach.h: TWO BUDDHAS ON THE OLD ROADS.
teach.b: The Bamiyan valley sat on the old roads between India and Central Asia, the roads monks and merchants walked.

Buddhist communities carved the two standing Buddhas into the cliff, with caves around them where monks lived and meditated, some painted inside. We've met the pilgrim Xuanzang, who walked from China to India for texts.
He passed through Bamiyan, and his record describes a great standing Buddha carved from the rock, its gold shining, and monasteries with monks. His few lines let us see the valley when it was alive.
Over the centuries the region's people changed faiths, and the statues stayed, worn by weather, time and earlier damage, their faces long gone, but standing.

teach.h: DESTROYED, DESPITE PLEAS TO SPARE THEM.
teach.b: Then, within living memory, the Taliban, who ruled Afghanistan at the time, declared the statues idols and destroyed them with explosives.
People of many faiths around the world, Muslims among them, had asked that they be spared. They were not.

teach.h: THE SHAPE OF WHERE IT'S GONE.
teach.b: The two empty niches are still there, the shape of the Buddhas pressed into the rock like a footprint. The Buddha taught impermanence: everything put together comes apart. That teaching doesn't make the loss small.
It's still a loss, and people still grieve it.
But the niches say something too. You can see exactly what was there, by the shape of where it's gone.

how: Buddhists and others remember the Bamiyan Buddhas as a lost holy site and part of the world's shared heritage; the empty niches and the painted caves around them are now protected and visited.

o: an old kingdom in the far north of India
a mountain pass between Tibet and Nepal
an Afghan valley where two great Buddhas stood

p: the pilgrim who saw them shining
the shape where the Buddhas stood

s: the Bamiyan Buddhas were statues brought in and set up in the valley
they were carved from the cliff itself.
the pilgrim Xuanzang described a great standing Buddha at Bamiyan
his record of the journey tells of the statue and its shining gold.
once the statues were destroyed, nothing of them could be seen
the two empty niches remain, holding the shape of the Buddhas in the rock.

games.q: you visit Bamiyan today. the Buddhas are gone; two empty niches stand in the cliff. what do the niches show you?
o: exactly what was there, by the shape of where it's gone.
games.why: the hollows keep the outline of the Buddhas pressed into the rock, like a footprint.

practice: Bring to mind something that's gone, a building you loved, a place that changed, a voice, and don't rush to fix the feeling; just look at the shape it left, the way the niches hold the shape of the Buddhas.
Say silently: I remember you. Then rest in the breath, and let the remembering be enough.

wordCard.voice: Bamiyan. The Afghan valley where two great Buddhas stood in the cliff, seen by Xuanzang, destroyed in our own time, and remembered in their empty niches.

carryVoice: Your line: the empty niches. Impermanence doesn't make a loss small. Day nine hundred forty-two, done.
